newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Sept 24.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Sept 24.

text.p: - Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- CUNARD SALE CONFIRMED BY WARD

Recently resigned Cunard chairman Peter Ward has confirmed the luxury cruise line is for sale. Mr Ward will remain in his post until the end of next month. Discussions with potential buyers are continuing, with no agreement imminent. An outright sale of the group is unlikely because it would prove to be too difficult to find a buyer willing to take on the loss- making company. Cunard had a 16 million stg operating loss last year.
-- PRICE RISES RAIL TO END FUEL WARS

Figures show that petrol prices have risen five times in as many weeks as oil companies try to pass on higher costs and cut losses. Esso, Shell and British Petroleum have insisted that the increases did not signal an end to the year- long price war but companies have been attempting to improve depressed margins. Industry estimates suggest the price war is achieving part of its objective in reducing the share of the petrol market held by the retailers.
-- FBI PROBE INTO LEAK OF INTEREST RATE TALKS

The source of a leak that eight out of 12 Federal Reserve regional bank presidents have recommended a rise in interest rates is to be investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. This is the second time the FBI has investigated such a leak and the move is an indication of how seriously Fed officials take the report, which was published on the Reuter newswire last week. It caused bond prices to fall and market interest rates to jump.
THE TIMES
-- FIFTY NAMES FACE ONE MILLION STG WRITS AS LLOYD'S GETS TOUGH

Authorities at Lloyd's of London are to harden their attitude towards 50 Lloyd's Names by pursuing them for more than one million stg. The Names will face total financial ruin, which will see bank accounts frozen and lead to the seizure of homes and assets. The Names will be disclosed early next month and will include well-known personalities in the UK and North America. Lloyd's is seeking 500 million stg from 1,850 Names.
-- RATE FEARS HIT MARKETS

The Federal Open Market Committee is due to meet today with the anticipation of a rise in the US interest rates, which has led the stock markets of Europe and America to fall sharply. If the Fed acts, it would be the first American interest rate rise since January 1995. The debate on either side of the Atlantic is over whether interest rate rises would help to control any emerging inflationary pressures or spoil the prospects of further economic growth.
-- UK FACES DISRUPTION ON EMU PLANNING

A report published by the British Bankers' Association suggests that the UK economy could be facing serious disruption if the Government fails to make a clear decision on whether it will participate in the process of European Monetary Union after other Governments have made their choices. The report says those most in danger from a delayed decision could be retailers and motor manufacturers. BAA director general Tim Sweeney says that whether or not the UK joins EMU the money and derivatives markets or London's position at the centre of global trading will not be affected.
THE GUARDIAN
-- BA DEAL ESCAPES MONOPOLY INQUIRY

Ministers have decided not to refer the considered alliance between British Airways and American Airlines to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission. However, BA will be expected to return to relinquish its hold on access to Heathrow airport, which will open up slots for American airlines and pave the way for an "open skies" agreement with the US government. Ian Lang, the Trade and Industry Secretary, is expected to approve the deal as early as next week.
-- BANK CLIENTS FEEL CALLED TO PHONE

According to a new report on retail banking from the consultancy Datamonitor, one-third of bank customers will bank by phone by the year 2000. The report says that the number of regular users will triple to ten million by the end of the century, with 125,000 people a month switching to telephone banking. The consultancy also predicts that telephone banking calls would rise from 41.3 million a year in 1995 to 130 million a year by 2000.
-- TWO QUIT CHRYSALIS BOARD AFTER ROW OVER ENDING FILM ACTIVITIES

Film producer Sir David Puttnam and Viscount Chandos, two non-executive directors at Chrysalis, have decided to leave the board in protest over the lack of communication in the way the company decided to close its film business, which has cost about four million stg. Chrysalis blamed tough trading conditions for the decision to pull out of the film business. Chairman of Chrysalis Chris Wright said replacements would be announced as soon as possible.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- ANGER AS HESELTINE CONSIDERS REMOVAL OF JOB SAFEGUARDS

Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine has said that ministers were starting a consultation exercise to examine whether small firms should be exempt from some employment rights. The legislation would affect firms employing ten workers or fewer. The Labour Party issued a warning that this could lead to half of the UK workforce losing the right to redundancy pay and compensation for unfair dismissal.
-- LLOYDS TSB TO CUT JOBS AS INSURANCE ARMS MERGE

The merger of Lloyds TSB's TSB and Abbey Life insurance arms could lead to the loss of hundreds of jobs. Lloyds TSB announced last week that it planned to buy up the remaining stake in Lloyds Abbey Life, a majority-owned insurance venture. Chief executive and chairman designate Sir Brian Pitman said the bank was determined to expand its insurance operations and would consider further acquisitions in the sector.
-- PROFIT WARNING PUTS BERISFORD UNDER PRESSURE

The City has put pressure on the management at Berisford, the Magnet kitchens to catering equipment group, after a profits warning sent shares in the group to a three-year low. Last month Berisford said that workers at Magnet's Darlington factory had voted for strike action, thus affecting production. Analysts were also stunned by the news that Welbilt, a US manufacturer of commercial kitchen equipment for McDonalds and Burger King, had been hit by a series of problems ranging from lower demand to difficulties with a new computer system.
